blocks.content: Most collections you reach for every day, a HashMap, an ArrayList, a plain dictionary, were never designed with threads in mind. They assume one caller at a time, reading and writing in a predictable order.
The moment two threads touch the same collection at the same time, that assumption breaks quietly. Nothing crashes right away. The map just starts lying to you.

This lesson looks at why ordinary collections fall apart under concurrent access, what it costs to fix that with a single big lock, and how purpose built concurrent collections do better by spreading the work instead of serializing all of it.
By the end you should be able to look at an access pattern, mostly reads or mostly writes, and pick a collection that fits it instead of reaching for the same lock every time.

An ordinary collection is unsafe to share across threads because its internal state, size counters, bucket arrays, next pointers, can be read and written half updated at the same time, corrupting the structure itself, not just the data inside it.
1. Why a plain collection is not thread safe
blocks.text: 1. Why a plain collection is not thread safe

blocks.content: A HashMap is not just a container of key value pairs. It is a data structure with internal invariants: a bucket array, a size count, chains or trees inside each bucket, and pointers that link entries together.
Every method call on that map assumes it starts from a consistent state and leaves a consistent state behind. When only one thread ever calls those methods, that assumption always holds.
Add a second thread and the assumption stops holding. Two threads can both decide a bucket needs to grow, both start resizing, and stomp on each other halfway through.

blocks.content: What actually goes wrong
blocks.text: What actually goes wrong

blocks.content: ["Lost updates: two threads read the same counter, both add one, and only one increment survives.","Torn resizes: a HashMap growing its bucket array while another thread reads from it can produce an infinite loop or a silently dropped entry.","Visibility gaps: a write on one thread may sit in a CPU cache and never become visible to a thread running on another core.","Iterator corruption: mutating a list while another thread iterates it can throw or, worse, just skip elements silently."]
items: Lost updates: two threads read the same counter, both add one, and only one increment survives.
Torn resizes: a HashMap growing its bucket array while another thread reads from it can produce an infinite loop or a silently dropped entry.
Visibility gaps: a write on one thread may sit in a CPU cache and never become visible to a thread running on another core.
Iterator corruption: mutating a list while another thread iterates it can throw or, worse, just skip elements silently.

blocks.title: This is not about "usually fine"
blocks.content: Under low contention a broken plain collection might work for months. The bugs surface under load, in production, at the worst possible time, because that is exactly when two threads are most likely to overlap.
The fix people reach for first is a lock. Wrap every operation on the shared collection in the same lock, and only one thread can be inside at a time.
A broken shared HashMap
blocks.text: A broken shared HashMap

blocks.content: Here is the failure in code. Multiple threads increment counters in a plain map with no synchronization at all.

codes.python:
import threading

counts = {}

def increment(key):
    current = counts.get(key, 0)
    counts[key] = current + 1

def worker():
    for _ in range(100000):
        increment("clicks")

t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker)
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()
# CPython's GIL protects individual bytecode ops but not this
# read-modify-write sequence, so the final count is often short.
print(counts.get("clicks"))

blocks.content: Run this a few times and the printed count drifts. Two threads read the same value, both compute the same next value, and one increment vanishes.
2. Wrapping everything in one big lock
blocks.text: 2. Wrapping everything in one big lock

blocks.content: The obvious fix is to put a single lock around the shared collection and require every thread to hold that lock before touching it.
This is called coarse grained locking, one lock guards the whole structure, regardless of which part of it a given operation actually touches.
Why it works
blocks.text: Why it works

blocks.content: With one lock, only one thread can be inside the collection at any moment. All the interleavings that produced torn resizes and lost updates simply cannot happen anymore, because there is no second thread present to interleave with.
Why it is expensive
blocks.text: Why it is expensive

blocks.content: ["Every read now competes with every write for the same lock, even reads to completely different keys.","Threads spend time waiting instead of working, and that wait time grows with thread count.","A single slow operation, one big resize, holds the lock and stalls every other thread that wanted the map.","Throughput stops scaling once you add more cores, because the lock is now the bottleneck, not the CPU."]
items: Every read now competes with every write for the same lock, even reads to completely different keys.
Threads spend time waiting instead of working, and that wait time grows with thread count.
A single slow operation, one big resize, holds the lock and stalls every other thread that wanted the map.
Throughput stops scaling once you add more cores, because the lock is now the bottleneck, not the CPU.

blocks.content: Fixing the counter with one coarse lock
blocks.text: Fixing the counter with one coarse lock

blocks.content: This version is correct. It is also strictly serial: no two threads ever run inside the map at the same time.

codes.python:
import threading

counts = {}
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment(key):
    with lock:
        current = counts.get(key, 0)
        counts[key] = current + 1

def worker():
    for _ in range(100000):
        increment("clicks")

t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker)
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()
print(counts.get("clicks"))  # always 200000, but slower under load

blocks.content: Correctness is fixed, but so is the concurrency. Two threads incrementing different, unrelated keys still take turns waiting on the same single lock.

blocks.title: Coarse locking is a valid starting point
blocks.content: It is simple, it is obviously correct, and it is a fine choice when contention is low. The problem only shows up once many threads genuinely need to work at the same time.
3. ConcurrentHashMap and how it does better
blocks.text: 3. ConcurrentHashMap and how it does better

blocks.content: Java's ConcurrentHashMap solves the same correctness problem without forcing every operation through one lock.
The core idea, lock striping and per bucket coordination
blocks.text: The core idea, lock striping and per bucket coordination

blocks.content: Instead of one lock for the whole map, the internal state is split so that unrelated operations can proceed independently. Modern versions synchronize at the level of an individual bucket, using compare and swap for the common cases and a small per bin lock only when a bucket actually has to change shape.
Two threads updating different keys usually land in different buckets and never contend with each other at all. They only block if they happen to target the same bucket at the same instant.
Reads do not block at all
blocks.text: Reads do not block at all

blocks.content: Get operations on a ConcurrentHashMap generally do not take a lock. They rely on volatile reads and careful publication of updated nodes, so a reader sees either the old value or the new one, never a torn one, without ever waiting.
Atomic compound operations
blocks.text: Atomic compound operations

blocks.content: ConcurrentHashMap also exposes methods like putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, and merge, which perform a whole read-modify-write sequence atomically, inside the map itself, so callers never need their own external lock for these common patterns.
Fixing the counter properly with ConcurrentHashMap
blocks.text: Fixing the counter properly with ConcurrentHashMap

blocks.content: This version scales because unrelated keys stop contending with each other.

codes.python:
# Python's queue module is the standard purpose built concurrent
# structure: a thread safe queue with its own internal lock and
# condition variables, tuned for the producer, consumer pattern
# rather than for arbitrary map access.
import queue
import threading

work_queue = queue.Queue()

def producer():
    for i in range(100000):
        work_queue.put(i)

def consumer(results):
    total = 0
    while True:
        item = work_queue.get()
        if item is None:
            break
        total += 1
    results.append(total)

results = []
t1 = threading.Thread(target=producer)
t1.start()
t1.join()
work_queue.put(None)
t2 = threading.Thread(target=consumer, args=(results,))
t2.start()
t2.join()
print(results)

blocks.content: Correctness is preserved, and threads working on different keys no longer wait for each other.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494848703-126157013.png
blocks.alt: One coarse lock forcing every thread through a single gate around a plain HashMap

blocks.content: The diagram above shows the coarse lock world: every thread funnels through one gate before it can touch the map, no matter which key it wants.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494850476-301209401.png
blocks.alt: A concurrent map letting threads work through separate segments in parallel

blocks.content: Compare that to a concurrent map, where each thread can proceed through its own segment of the structure, and only threads that collide on the same segment ever wait on each other.
4. CopyOnWriteArrayList and when it fits
blocks.text: 4. CopyOnWriteArrayList and when it fits

blocks.content: Lists have a different shape of problem. Iterating a list while another thread mutates it is one of the most common sources of concurrent bugs.

CopyOnWriteArrayList takes a different approach entirely. Every mutation, add, remove, set, makes a full copy of the underlying array, changes the copy, and then swaps the internal reference to point at the new array.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512253699-235489094.png
blocks.alt: CopyOnWriteArrayList writer copying the array, appending the new element and swapping the reference while a reader keeps iterating the old snapshot

blocks.content: Why iteration becomes trivial
blocks.text: Why iteration becomes trivial

blocks.content: Because the array reference is only ever swapped, never mutated in place, an iterator created before a write keeps looking at the old array for as long as it runs. It never sees a partial update and it never throws a concurrent modification exception.
The cost of that guarantee
blocks.text: The cost of that guarantee

blocks.content: ["Every write copies the entire backing array, so writes are O(n) instead of O(1).","Memory churns under frequent writes, since each mutation allocates a whole new array.","It only pays off when reads vastly outnumber writes, think configuration lists or listener registries that change rarely but get iterated constantly."]
items: Every write copies the entire backing array, so writes are O(n) instead of O(1).
Memory churns under frequent writes, since each mutation allocates a whole new array.
It only pays off when reads vastly outnumber writes, think configuration lists or listener registries that change rarely but get iterated constantly.

blocks.title: A listener registry
blocks.text: A pub-sub system keeps a list of event listeners. New listeners are added rarely, maybe a few times at startup. But every incoming event iterates the whole list to notify each listener. CopyOnWriteArrayList is a strong fit here: cheap frequent reads, rare and acceptable expensive writes, and no risk of a listener being added mid-iteration crashing the notify loop.

blocks.content: CopyOnWriteArrayList in practice
blocks.text: CopyOnWriteArrayList in practice

codes.python:
# Python does not ship a copy-on-write list in the standard
# library. The closest equivalent pattern is to hold a lock only
# long enough to snapshot the list, then iterate the snapshot
# without holding the lock at all.
import threading

class ListenerRegistry:
    def __init__(self):
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._listeners = []

    def subscribe(self, listener):
        with self._lock:
            self._listeners = self._listeners + [listener]

    def publish(self):
        # Read the reference once; a concurrent subscribe() replaces
        # the whole list rather than mutating this one.
        snapshot = self._listeners
        for listener in snapshot:
            listener()

blocks.content: 5. Choosing a structure for read heavy versus write heavy access
blocks.text: 5. Choosing a structure for read heavy versus write heavy access

blocks.content: The right concurrent collection depends entirely on how the collection actually gets used, not on which one sounds the most advanced.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512255552-952837636.png
blocks.alt: Access pattern branching into read heavy, balanced or write heavy, and producer consumer handoff, each pointing at the concurrent collection that fits

blocks.content: Read heavy, write rare
blocks.text: Read heavy, write rare

blocks.content: CopyOnWriteArrayList, or an immutable snapshot swapped behind a volatile reference, fits here. Reads are lock free and cheap. Writes are expensive but infrequent enough that the cost barely matters.
Balanced or write heavy maps
blocks.text: Balanced or write heavy maps

blocks.content: ConcurrentHashMap fits here. It gives lock free or low contention reads and writes that only block within a small slice of the structure, so throughput keeps scaling as you add threads.
Producer, consumer handoff
blocks.text: Producer, consumer handoff

blocks.content: A BlockingQueue in Java, or the queue module in Python, fits here. These are built around threads waiting for work to appear or waiting for space to free up, using condition variables internally instead of spinning or busy waiting.
Single threaded environments
blocks.text: Single threaded environments

blocks.content: In JavaScript's typical runtime, the event loop already guarantees that synchronous code never interleaves, so plain objects and arrays are safe without any concurrent collection at all. The concern only returns with worker threads and shared memory, where Atomics and SharedArrayBuffer take over the role locks play elsewhere.

6. Worked example, an in-memory cache under load
blocks.text: 6. Worked example, an in-memory cache under load

blocks.content: Say you are building a small in-memory cache that many request handling threads read from constantly, and a background refresh thread updates every few seconds.
Step 1, identify the access pattern
blocks.text: Step 1, identify the access pattern

blocks.content: Reads vastly outnumber writes. Every incoming request reads the cache. Only the refresh thread writes, and only occasionally.
Step 2, rule out a plain collection
blocks.text: Step 2, rule out a plain collection

blocks.content: A plain HashMap would corrupt under concurrent reads and writes the moment refresh overlaps with a request thread's read, exactly the torn read problem from section 1.
Step 3, rule out one coarse lock
blocks.text: Step 3, rule out one coarse lock

blocks.content: A single lock around the whole cache would force every request thread to wait in line just to read a value, even though they are not writing anything. That throttles the busiest part of the system to protect the rarest part.
Step 4, pick ConcurrentHashMap
blocks.text: Step 4, pick ConcurrentHashMap

blocks.content: ConcurrentHashMap gives lock free reads for the request threads and safe, isolated updates for the refresh thread, which is exactly the shape of this workload.

Notice that the Python version still needs a lock, because the standard library has no ConcurrentHashMap equivalent, but the critical section is tiny and fast, which keeps contention low even without fine grained internal striping.
7. Common pitfalls when switching to concurrent collections
blocks.text: 7. Common pitfalls when switching to concurrent collections

blocks.content: Assuming atomic pieces add up to an atomic whole
blocks.text: Assuming atomic pieces add up to an atomic whole

blocks.content: A get followed by a put on a ConcurrentHashMap is still two separate atomic operations, not one. Another thread can write between them. Use merge, compute, or putIfAbsent instead of hand rolling that sequence.
Iterating and expecting the latest data
blocks.text: Iterating and expecting the latest data

blocks.content: Iterators over concurrent collections are typically weakly consistent. They reflect the state at some point during iteration, not necessarily every update made after the iterator was created.
Mixing a concurrent collection with an external lock
blocks.text: Mixing a concurrent collection with an external lock

blocks.content: Wrapping a ConcurrentHashMap in your own coarse lock throws away everything it was built to give you. If you need multi step atomicity across several keys, that is a sign you need a different design, not a bigger lock.

["Prefer atomic compound methods over separate read then write calls.","Do not assume iteration order or freshness guarantees you did not explicitly verify.","Only add external locking for operations that truly span multiple keys or multiple collections."]
items: Prefer atomic compound methods over separate read then write calls.
Do not assume iteration order or freshness guarantees you did not explicitly verify.
Only add external locking for operations that truly span multiple keys or multiple collections.

blocks.content: 8. Rule of thumb for picking a concurrent collection
blocks.text: 8. Rule of thumb for picking a concurrent collection

blocks.content: Start by counting reads against writes, not by picking the most impressive sounding structure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512257413-246268742.png
blocks.alt: Decision flow for the rule of thumb, count reads versus writes, then check whether atomic compound operations or a producer consumer handoff are needed

blocks.content: The short version
blocks.text: The short version

blocks.content: ["Reads dominate and writes are rare: reach for CopyOnWriteArrayList or an immutable snapshot swap.","Reads and writes are both frequent on a map: reach for ConcurrentHashMap.","Threads hand work to each other: reach for a blocking queue.","You are in a single threaded JavaScript context: plain collections are already safe, save concurrent tools for worker threads.","You only need a single counter or flag: reach for an atomic primitive before reaching for any collection at all."]
items: Reads dominate and writes are rare: reach for CopyOnWriteArrayList or an immutable snapshot swap.
Reads and writes are both frequent on a map: reach for ConcurrentHashMap.
Threads hand work to each other: reach for a blocking queue.
You are in a single threaded JavaScript context: plain collections are already safe, save concurrent tools for worker threads.
You only need a single counter or flag: reach for an atomic primitive before reaching for any collection at all.

blocks.title: When in doubt, measure
blocks.content: Contention is easy to guess wrong. If you are unsure whether coarse locking is actually a bottleneck, measure it under realistic load before reaching for a more complex structure you do not yet need.
Ordinary collections are not broken, they were simply never asked to be shared. Concurrent collections exist because a single lock treats every operation the same, while real workloads rarely do.
Match the collection to the shape of your access pattern, and thread safety stops being something you bolt on and becomes something the structure already gives you.
